video.title: OpenAI solving Navier-Stokes explained..
video.genre: AI explainer and opinion, partly screen-shared

protocol.note: Drafted from the transcript alone, without seeing any jevcut output or other labels.
protocol.times_from: Lemonfox transcript; seconds in the source, so labels survive re-transcription

clips.why: Hook: the OpenAI Navier-Stokes controversy isn't because the equation is flawed -- it works in engineering, but it's never been proven to work in all conditions: 'literally the million-dollar question', open for decades. States the problem (always smooth in 3D, or a blow-up?), two ways to settle it, and lands at 274.8: OpenAI claims the second, a counterexample where the equation blows up. Later end (291.2, 75.2s) adds 10,000 agents / 130B tokens and 'sets precedent'; one 'as you can see' screen aside at ~254.

Hook: rumor that OpenAI is already moving past Navier-Stokes to other Millennium Prize problems. Makes us rethink human credit; the prize rules only allow a person or group of people, not an AI agent; payoff question at 652.1: between compute-rich labs doing the work and institutions giving direction, who deserves the attribution? Two starts both work: 579.6 opens on the stronger 'who will have the means to make scientific discoveries -- companies running 10,000 agents?' (72.5s); 593.4 on 'the world is full of unsolved questions' also fine. Preferred is the shortest.

Hook: 'to understand why researchers are claiming that OpenAI cheated...' Story: Euler's version ignores viscosity; Buckmaster (with Anthropic's Alpoglu) spent a year and found a *forced* blow-up; OpenAI heard, threw compute at the same problem and found an unforced one in 50 hours with 100 agents; payoff: plagiarism rumors because the approach was so similar. Can't land in 75s without losing the forced/unforced setup the punchline needs.

also_ok.why: Cold open on F=ma tied to OpenAI's Navier-Stokes claim; elevator worked example; solids move as one body, water doesn't; applying Newton's second law to fluid gives Navier-Stokes (ends before 'looks something like this'). Clear explainer but the elevator arithmetic makes it long.

negatives.why: Equation components read off the screen ('as you can see', 'this side of the equation'); the garden-hose and funnel examples sound clippable but annotate an on-screen formula.
'Underlying this entire scandal around OpenAI alleged cheating...' -- a thesis about compute and discovery stated before the scandal has been explained, then segues into the sponsor.
Counterexample visual ('visually it looks something like this', spiral vortex, 'like a tornado'): describes the on-screen render.
Text-message drama (88 hours, offer to drop Alpoglu's name, peeking at Codex history): juicy, but opens 'OpenAI went further than this' and assumes the Buckmaster story already told.
